etymology: Hebrew 'eseq, “contention” or “strife,” from a root meaning to quarrel or press upon another; the name Isaac gave the first well the herdmen of Gerar strove for.
biblical_def: When Isaac’s servants digged in the valley of Gerar and found a well of springing water, the herdmen of Gerar strove with them, saying, The water is ours; and Isaac called the name of the well Esek, “Contention,” “because they strove with him” (Gen 26:20). Isaac had the right, for his father Abraham had digged those wells before him; yet the heir of promise did not stand upon his right nor answer strife with strife. He yielded the well and removed to dig again. Here is the meekness that inherits the earth, the temper the Lord blessed when He said, Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth. The world reckons such yielding weakness; the covenant reckons it faith, for the man who trusts the LORD to make room for him need not seize a well by force. Esek stands as a monument to the peaceable heir who would rather lose a cistern than lose his peace, who overcomes not by contending but by giving place. In this Isaac was a son after the pattern of the greater Son, who, when He was reviled, reviled not again, but committed Himself to Him that judgeth righteously. The wells of the flesh are worth striving for only to the flesh; the child of promise digs, and if men take it, digs again, and waits upon the God who has wells enough.
webster_summary: The first well Isaac digged in the valley of Gerar, named “Contention” because the herdmen of Gerar strove for it (Gen 26:20); a monument to the meek heir who yields his right rather than strive.
webster_full: ESEK, a well in the valley of Gerar, the name signifying “contention.”
So called because the herdmen of Gerar strove with Isaac’s herdmen for the water (Gen 26:20).
Isaac held the right, yet yielded the well and removed to dig again.
A pattern of the meekness that inherits the earth and overcomes by giving place.
It stands over against Sitnah and Rehoboth as the first of Isaac’s three wells.
scriptures: And the herdmen of Gerar did strive with Isaac's herdmen, saying, The water is ours: and he called the name of the well Esek; because they strove with him.
And they digged another well, and strove for that also: and he called the name of it Sitnah.

And he removed from thence, and digged another well; and for that they strove not: and he called the name of it Rehoboth; and he said, For now the LORD hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land.
Gen 12:3
And I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.
corruption_summary: The well of contention where Isaac yielded rather than strove; it recovers the meekness of faith that trusts God to make room.
corruption_paragraphs: Esek is a well in the wilderness of Gerar, and no man now disputes its memory as the herdmen once disputed its water. The name preserves a plain fact: Isaac had the right to the well, and Isaac gave it up rather than answer strife with strife.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the meekness that inherits the earth. The world counts yielding as weakness, but the covenant counts it faith; the man who trusts the LORD to make room need not seize a well by force. Learn of Isaac to give place, and of the greater Son who, when reviled, reviled not again.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew root meaning to contend, quarrel, or press upon; the noun names the strife itself.
roots_lines: Esek renders Hebrew 'eseq, “contention.”
The root 'asaq means to quarrel, contend, or press upon another.
The same root touches the idea of oppression and wrongful seizure.
Isaac fixed the sense by naming the well for the strife of the herdmen.
Kin in theme, though not in root, to Sitnah, “hatred,” the next well.
usage: Isaac called the first well Esek, because they strove with him.
The strife of Esek did not move the patient heir to wrath.
Every believer meets an Esek before he comes to his Rehoboth.

etymology: Hebrew sitnah, “hatred” or “enmity,” from the root satan, to be an adversary; the name Isaac gave the second well, whose root stands also behind the name Satan.
biblical_def: No sooner had Isaac yielded the well of Esek than his servants digged another, and the herdmen of Gerar strove for that also; and he called the name of it Sitnah, “Hatred” (Gen 26:21). The name is heavy: it is not mere contention now but enmity, the settled malice of the world against the seed of promise. The same root stands behind Satan, the accuser and adversary; and every child of Abraham learns that the serpent’s enmity, first spoken in Eden, follows the covenant line from well to well. Isaac had done no wrong; he sought only water in a dry land, and for this he was hated. So it has ever been: the world hated the Master, and it hates the servants for His sake, without a cause. Yet mark the patience of the man of faith. He does not curse his enemies nor call down fire; he digs, and being wronged, digs again, leaving his cause with the LORD. Sitnah teaches the saints not to marvel that the world hates them, nor to render hatred for hatred, but to possess their souls in patience under repeated wrong. The enmity is real, and it is old, and it will not be reconciled this side of glory; but the God of Isaac gives wells enough, and the meek who endure shall yet dwell in the room the LORD prepares.
webster_summary: Isaac’s second well in the valley of Gerar, named “Hatred” because the herdmen strove for it also (Gen 26:21); a witness to the world’s enmity against the seed of promise and the patience that endures it.
webster_full: SITNAH, the second well digged by Isaac, the name signifying “hatred” or “enmity.”
The herdmen of Gerar strove for it also, so that contention deepened into malice (Gen 26:21).
Its root satan, to be an adversary, stands behind the name of the great Adversary.
It marks the old enmity of the world against the church, hated without a cause.
Isaac answered it not with cursing but with patience, digging yet again.
scriptures: And they digged another well, and strove for that also: and he called the name of it Sitnah.
And the herdmen of Gerar did strive with Isaac's herdmen, saying, The water is ours: and he called the name of the well Esek; because they strove with him.

And he removed from thence, and digged another well; and for that they strove not: and he called the name of it Rehoboth; and he said, For now the LORD hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land.
Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people.
corruption_summary: The well of hatred where Isaac endured wrong without rendering wrong; it recovers patience under the world’s enmity.
corruption_paragraphs: Sitnah is a well in a dry land, and its name is enmity. The herdmen of Gerar were not content to have taken Esek; they pursued their hatred to the next well also, that Isaac might learn how the world receives the friends of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is patience under hatred without cause. The saints are not to marvel that the world hates them, nor to answer malice with malice, but to leave their cause with the LORD and dig again. The enmity is ancient and will not be reconciled this side of glory, yet the God of Isaac gives wells enough.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew satan, to bear enmity or act as an adversary; the noun names hatred itself.
roots_lines: Sitnah renders Hebrew sitnah, “hatred” or “enmity.”
The root satan means to be an adversary or to accuse.
The same root gives the name Satan, the accuser of the brethren.
A cognate form names the accusation brought against Judah in Ezra 4:6.
Isaac fixed the sense by naming the well for the malice of the herdmen.
usage: The second well he called Sitnah, for the strife had turned to hatred.
Sitnah is the enmity the world bears the seed of promise.
He met his Sitnah with patience, and left the wrong with God.

etymology: Hebrew Rehoboth, “room” or “broad places,” from the root rachab, to be wide or enlarged; the third well Isaac digged, for which the herdmen strove not.
biblical_def: After the strife of Esek and the hatred of Sitnah came the well of rest. Isaac removed from thence and digged another well, and for that they strove not; and he called the name of it Rehoboth, saying, “For now the LORD hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land” (Gen 26:22). Three wells, and only at the third did strife cease — not because Isaac grew mighty enough to hold it, but because the LORD made room. This is the covenant way: the God who tries His people with contention and hatred at length enlarges their border, and gives peace after long patience. Rehoboth is broad places, the opposite of the strait and narrow pinch of the world’s enmity; it is the room God makes for those who would not make room for themselves by force. The patient heir who yielded two wells is given a third unmolested, and with it the promise of fruitfulness. So the pilgrim who trusts the LORD through Esek and Sitnah is brought at last into a large place: he brought me forth also into a large place; he delivered me, because he delighted in me. Every believer has his Rehoboth appointed, if he will but dig and wait; and the fullness of it is that eternal room in the Father’s house, where strife is forgotten and the children of promise are fruitful for ever.
webster_summary: Isaac’s third well, named “Room” because for it the herdmen strove not, the LORD having made room for His people (Gen 26:22); a witness that God enlarges the border of the patient after long striving.
webster_full: REHOBOTH, the third well digged by Isaac, the name signifying “room” or “broad places.”
For it the herdmen of Gerar strove not, and Isaac dwelt in peace (Gen 26:22).
Isaac named it saying, For now the LORD hath made room for us.
It follows Esek and Sitnah as the rest that comes after long patience.
Distinct from Rehoboth by the river, the Edomite city of Genesis 36.
scriptures: And he removed from thence, and digged another well; and for that they strove not: and he called the name of it Rehoboth; and he said, For now the LORD hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land.
And the herdmen of Gerar did strive with Isaac's herdmen, saying, The water is ours: and he called the name of the well Esek; because they strove with him.
And they digged another well, and strove for that also: and he called the name of it Sitnah.
Gen 12:3
And I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.
corruption_summary: The well of room where the LORD enlarged Isaac after strife; it recovers the truth that God makes room for the patient in His own time.
corruption_paragraphs: Rehoboth is the well of Isaac in the wilderness south of Gerar, and it is to be distinguished from Rehoboth by the river, the ancient city of Edom named in the generations of Esau. This entry is the well of the peaceable heir, where the LORD made room after two wells had been wrested away.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD makes room for His people, and gives fruitfulness after long patience. Men strive to enlarge themselves by force; the child of promise digs and waits, and the God who delighteth in him brings him forth into a large place. Every believer has his Rehoboth appointed.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew rachab, to be wide or enlarged; the plural noun names broad and roomy places.
roots_lines: Rehoboth renders Hebrew Rehoboth, “room” or “broad places.”
The root rachab means to be or grow wide, to enlarge.
The related noun rechob names the broad open street of a city.
The same root gives the sense of enlargement in prayer and deliverance.
The name marks the enlarging hand of the LORD upon the patient heir.
usage: He called the third well Rehoboth, for the LORD had made room.
After Esek and Sitnah, Isaac dwelt in the peace of Rehoboth.
The saint finds his Rehoboth when God at last enlarges his border.

etymology: Hebrew Gal'ed, “the heap of witness,” from gal, a heap, and 'ed, a witness; Jacob’s Hebrew name for the memorial heap Laban called in Aramaic Jegarsahadutha.
biblical_def: When Jacob and Laban made their covenant of parting in the hill country of Gilead, they gathered stones into a heap; and Laban called it in his Syrian tongue Jegarsahadutha, but Jacob called it Galeed — both names meaning “the heap of witness” (Gen 31:47). “And Laban said, This heap is a witness between me and thee this day. Therefore was the name of it called Galeed” (Gen 31:48). Two suspicious men, each mistrusting the other, could agree upon one thing: that God saw between them. The heap could not speak, but it stood as a silent testimony that the LORD watched when men were parted and out of one another’s sight. Here is the doctrine of the covenant-witness. Men make vows and pass beyond each other’s reach, but there is no border God does not oversee, no promise sworn that heaven does not record. Galeed preaches that the LORD is Himself the witness to every covenant, the Judge who marks the keeping and the breaking of it; and this is a terror to the false and a comfort to the true. The believer walks in the sight of that same Witness, and orders his dealings as one who knows that a heap of stones, or the searching eye of God, will testify at the last. Let every vow be made as unto Him who watcheth between, and every parting be sealed by His faithfulness rather than man’s.
webster_summary: The heap of stones Jacob raised as a witness of his covenant with Laban, named in Hebrew “the heap of witness” (Gen 31:47–48); a monument that the LORD watches between men who are parted.
webster_full: GALEED, a heap of stones in Gilead, the name signifying “the heap of witness.”
Jacob so named it when he and Laban made their covenant of parting (Gen 31:47).
Laban called it in Aramaic Jegarsahadutha, of the very same meaning.
This heap is a witness between me and thee this day, said Laban (Gen 31:48).
It preaches that the LORD is witness to every vow and watches between parted men.
scriptures: And Laban called it Jegarsahadutha: but Jacob called it Galeed.
And Laban said, This heap is a witness between me and thee this day. Therefore was the name of it called Galeed;
Gen 12:3
And I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.
Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people.
corruption_summary: The heap of witness between Jacob and Laban; it recovers the truth that God is witness to every covenant and watches between men who are parted.
corruption_paragraphs: Galeed is a heap of common stones, gathered in an hour of mutual mistrust, and given the highest of names: a witness. Jacob and Laban, who trusted each other little, agreed that the LORD saw between them, and set up the heap to remember it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD is the witness to every covenant and vow. Men pass beyond one another’s sight, but no promise is sworn that heaven does not record. Let every dealing be ordered before the eye that watcheth between, which is terror to the false and comfort to the true.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew gal, a heap, and 'ed, a witness; the compound names the heap raised to testify.
roots_lines: Galeed renders Hebrew Gal'ed, “the heap of witness.”
The word gal means a heap or pile, as of stones or waves.
The word 'ed means a witness or testimony.
Laban’s Aramaic Jegarsahadutha bears the identical meaning.
The name is akin to Gilead, the hill country where the heap was raised.
usage: Jacob called the heap Galeed, a witness between him and Laban.
The stones of Galeed could not speak, yet they testified before God.
As at Galeed, the LORD is witness to every covenant men make.

etymology: Hebrew Tab'erah, “a burning,” from the root ba'ar, to burn or kindle; the name given the camp where the fire of the LORD consumed the murmurers.
biblical_def: Scarcely had Israel departed from the mount of God when they fell to complaining, and it displeased the LORD; and the fire of the LORD burnt among them, and consumed them that were in the uttermost parts of the camp. “And he called the name of the place Taberah: because the fire of the LORD burnt among them” (Num 11:3). Moses set it among the places of provocation: “And at Taberah, and at Massah, and at Kibrothhattaavah, ye provoked the LORD to wrath” (Deu 9:22). The murmuring seemed a small thing to the people — only a complaint, a weariness of the way — but to the holy God it was contempt of His goodness and unbelief of His care, and He answered it with fire. Taberah stands as a warning against the sin that men count least: the discontented tongue. The same God who is a consuming fire against His enemies will not be mocked by the murmuring of His own; and the fire fell not upon the strangers but upon Israel, in the uttermost parts of the camp, where complaint festers farthest from the tabernacle. Let the pilgrim mark it well. Grumbling is not innocent; it chargeth God foolishly, and the New Testament sets Israel’s murmuring before us that we sin not as they did, when they were destroyed of the destroyer. Serve the LORD with gladness, lest the burning of Taberah be kindled again.
webster_summary: The wilderness camp where the fire of the LORD burnt among the murmuring people, named “A burning” (Num 11:3); a witness to the holy jealousy of God against the discontented tongue.
webster_full: TABERAH, a camp in the wilderness, the name signifying “a burning.”
So called because the fire of the LORD burnt among the murmuring people (Num 11:3).
It fell in the uttermost parts of the camp, farthest from the tabernacle.
Moses numbered it among the places where Israel provoked the LORD (Deu 9:22).
It warns that the discontented tongue is contempt of God’s goodness.
scriptures: Num 11:3
And he called the name of the place Taberah: because the fire of the LORD burnt among them.
Deu 9:22
And at Taberah, and at Massah, and at Kibrothhattaavah, ye provoked the LORD to wrath.
Psa 46:6
The heathen raged, the kingdoms were moved: he uttered his voice, the earth melted.
Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people.
corruption_summary: The place of burning where God answered murmuring with fire; it recovers the seriousness of the complaining tongue before a holy God.
corruption_paragraphs: Taberah is a camp in the wilderness of Paran, remembered for one dreadful reason: there the fire of the LORD burnt among the people because they murmured. The name itself is a sermon, fixing the judgment in the very ground.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the holy jealousy of God against complaining. Men reckon grumbling a light thing, a mere weariness of the way; but it chargeth God foolishly and despiseth His care. The apostle sets Israel’s murmuring before the church as a warning; serve the LORD with gladness, lest the burning be kindled again.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew ba'ar, to burn, kindle, or consume; the noun names the burning itself.
roots_lines: Taberah renders Hebrew Tab'erah, “a burning.”
The root ba'ar means to burn, kindle, or be consumed.
The same root describes the fire of the LORD and the wrath that burns.
It names the place by the judgment that fell there.
Near in theme to Massah and Kibroth-hattaavah, the other camps of provocation.
usage: He called the place Taberah, because the fire of the LORD burnt among them.
At Taberah the murmuring of the camp was answered with flame.
Let no man count grumbling harmless who remembers Taberah.

etymology: Hebrew Massah, “temptation” or “testing,” from the root nasah, to prove or put to the test; the name Moses gave the place at Rephidim for the sin of tempting God, distinct from Meribah, “strife.”
biblical_def: At Rephidim, where there was no water for the people to drink, Israel chode with Moses and tempted the LORD; and Moses called the name of the place Massah, and Meribah, “because they tempted the LORD, saying, Is the LORD among us, or not?” (Exo 17:7). One place bore two names for two sins: Meribah, “strife,” for their contention with Moses; and Massah, “temptation,” for their putting God to the proof. This entry marks the second — the sin of demanding that God prove Himself, as though His long faithfulness through plague and sea and manna counted for nothing the moment thirst returned. To ask, Is the LORD among us, or not, after such wonders, is not honest doubt but insolent unbelief, a challenge flung at heaven. Therefore the LORD wrote it into His law: “Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God, as ye tempted him in Massah” (Deu 6:16); and He remembered it against the honor of Levi, “whom thou didst prove at Massah” (Deu 33:8). Our Lord Himself took this very word to defeat the tempter, answering, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God. Where Israel demanded a sign, the true Israel refused to cast Himself down. Massah teaches the saint to rest on what God has done and said, and never to make faith hang upon a fresh proof extorted from His hand. He that believeth shall not make haste.
webster_summary: The place at Rephidim named “Temptation” because Israel tempted the LORD, saying, Is the LORD among us, or not (Exo 17:7); the same event as Meribah, but named for the distinct sin of putting God to the proof.
webster_full: MASSAH, a place at Rephidim, the name signifying “temptation” or “testing.”
So called because Israel tempted the LORD, saying, Is the LORD among us, or not (Exo 17:7).
It is the same event as Meribah, but named for tempting rather than striving.
The law forbade it: Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God, as in Massah (Deu 6:16).
Christ wielded this word against the tempter in the wilderness.
scriptures: Exo 17:7
And he called the name of the place Massah, and Meribah, because of the chiding of the children of Israel, and because they tempted the LORD, saying, Is the LORD among us, or not?
Deu 6:16
Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God, as ye tempted him in Massah.
Deu 33:8
And of Levi he said, Let thy Thummim and thy Urim be with thy holy one, whom thou didst prove at Massah, and with whom thou didst strive at the waters of Meribah;
Deu 9:22
And at Taberah, and at Massah, and at Kibrothhattaavah, ye provoked the LORD to wrath.
corruption_summary: The place of tempting God, the same as Meribah but named for the sin of testing rather than strife; it recovers the duty to rest on God’s proven word.
corruption_paragraphs: Massah and Meribah are one place at Rephidim, yet two names for two sins. Meribah is the strife of the people with Moses; Massah is their tempting of the LORD, putting Him to the proof as though His mighty works were nothing. This entry marks the sin of the test.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that faith rests on what God has done and said, and does not extort fresh proofs from His hand. To demand, Is the LORD among us, or not, after the sea and the manna, is insolent unbelief. Our Lord answered the tempter with this very word: Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew nasah, to test, prove, or put to trial; the noun names the temptation itself.
roots_lines: Massah renders Hebrew Massah, “temptation” or “testing.”
The root nasah means to test, try, or put to the proof.
God tries His people in faithfulness; the people tried God in unbelief.
The same root describes Abraham proved, and Israel proving the LORD.
Distinct in sense from Meribah, from rib, to strive or contend.
usage: He called the place Massah, because they tempted the LORD there.
Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God, as ye tempted him in Massah.
To demand a sign of God is the very sin of Massah.

etymology: Hebrew Nayoth, “dwellings” or “habitations,” from naveh, a dwelling or pasture; the prophetic quarters at Ramah where Samuel presided and David sheltered.
biblical_def: When Saul sought David’s life, David fled to Samuel at Ramah and told him all that Saul had done; “and he and Samuel went and dwelt in Naioth” (1Sa 19:18). Naioth was the dwellings, the habitations of the prophets gathered about Samuel, a house of prophesying and prayer; and it became a sanctuary for the anointed fugitive. Saul sent messengers to take David, and the Spirit of God came upon them, and they prophesied; he sent again, and again; and at the last Saul went himself, “and the Spirit of God was upon him also, and he went on, and prophesied, until he came to Naioth in Ramah” (1Sa 19:23). Behold the safety of the place where the LORD is worshipped. The persecutor’s arm is shortened at the threshold of prayer; the very soldiers sent to seize the servant of God are seized themselves by the Spirit, and the king who breathed out threatenings is stripped and made to prophesy in spite of himself. Naioth preaches that no weapon formed against the LORD’s anointed shall prosper, and that the Spirit who fell upon Saul that day can overpower the mightiest enemy of the church. God is able to defend His own without a sword drawn, turning the pursuer into a prophet and the arrows of malice into praise. The hidden strength of the saints is not in walls but in the presence of the God who dwells among His prophesying people.
webster_summary: The prophetic dwellings at Ramah where Samuel and David sheltered, and the Spirit of God overpowered even Saul’s messengers and Saul himself (1Sa 19:18–23); a witness to the safety of the LORD’s presence.
webster_full: NAIOTH, the prophetic dwellings at Ramah, the name signifying “habitations.”
There Samuel presided over the company of the prophets, and David fled thither (1Sa 19:18).
Saul’s messengers, sent to take David, were seized by the Spirit and prophesied.
Saul himself came, and the Spirit of God was upon him also (1Sa 19:23).
It shows that no weapon against the LORD’s anointed shall prosper.
scriptures: So David fled, and escaped, and came to Samuel to Ramah, and told him all that Saul had done to him. And he and Samuel went and dwelt in Naioth.
And he went thither to Naioth in Ramah: and the Spirit of God was upon him also, and he went on, and prophesied, until he came to Naioth in Ramah.

As the dew of Hermon, and as the dew that descended upon the mountains of Zion: for there the LORD commanded the blessing, even life for evermore.
corruption_summary: The prophetic dwellings where the Spirit overpowered the persecutor; it recovers the safety of the saints in the presence of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Naioth was the habitation of the prophets at Ramah, a house of prophesying about Samuel, and a refuge for David when Saul sought his life. There the Spirit of God fell upon the very men sent to seize him, and upon Saul himself.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD defends His own without a sword drawn. The persecutor’s arm is shortened at the threshold of prayer, and the Spirit who overpowered Saul can subdue the mightiest enemy of the church. The strength of the saints is not in walls but in the presence of God.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew naveh, a dwelling, habitation, or pasture; the plural form names the prophetic quarters.
roots_lines: Naioth renders Hebrew Nayoth, “dwellings” or “habitations.”
The root naveh means a dwelling, abode, or shepherd’s pasture.
It named the quarters where the sons of the prophets abode with Samuel.
The place is always joined to Ramah, Samuel’s own city.
A home of prophesying became a sanctuary for the anointed fugitive.
usage: David and Samuel went and dwelt in Naioth at Ramah.
At Naioth even Saul’s messengers were made to prophesy.
The safety of Naioth was the presence of God, not its walls.

etymology: Hebrew Seku, perhaps “the lookout” or “watchtower,” from a root meaning to look out or observe; a place near Ramah marked by a great well.
biblical_def: On the road to Ramah there stood a landmark known to all, the great well in Sechu; and thither came Saul in his hunt for David, and “he asked and said, Where are Samuel and David? And one said, Behold, they be at Naioth in Ramah” (1Sa 19:22). A small notice, yet full of instruction. Even the pursuer’s steps are ordered of the LORD; Saul comes to the well, asks his question, and is told plainly where the hunted men are — and yet he cannot lay a hand upon them, for the Spirit meets him before he arrives. The well of Sechu shows that God does not always hide His people by concealment; sometimes He lets the enemy know exactly where they are, that the deliverance may be the more manifestly His own. The wicked may learn the very place, and still be turned back at the door. Here is comfort for the saint who feels himself easily found and much exposed: it is not our hiddenness that keeps us, but our God. The steps of a good man are ordered by the LORD, and so, in another sense, are the steps of his enemy; Saul walks to Sechu, asks, is answered, and is undone. The LORD hides His own not always in the dark, but often in plain sight, under the shadow of His hand, where no malice can reach them till He please.
webster_summary: The place near Ramah with a great well where Saul asked after Samuel and David (1Sa 19:22); a witness that the pursuer’s steps are ordered, and the LORD hides His own even in plain sight.
webster_full: SECHU, a place near Ramah, notable for its great well.
Thither Saul came in pursuit of David and Samuel (1Sa 19:22).
At the well he asked, Where are Samuel and David, and was plainly told.
Yet he could not seize them, for the Spirit met him at Naioth.
It shows that the enemy’s steps are ordered, and God keeps His own.
scriptures: Then went he also to Ramah, and came to a great well that is in Sechu: and he asked and said, Where are Samuel and David? And one said, Behold, they be at Naioth in Ramah.
And he went thither to Naioth in Ramah: and the Spirit of God was upon him also, and he went on, and prophesied, until he came to Naioth in Ramah.
So David fled, and escaped, and came to Samuel to Ramah, and told him all that Saul had done to him. And he and Samuel went and dwelt in Naioth.
Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people.
corruption_summary: The well where the pursuer asked after the hunted, and still could not take them; it recovers the truth that God keeps His own even when the enemy knows the place.
corruption_paragraphs: Sechu is a place near Ramah, remembered for its great well and for one question asked there. Saul, hunting David, came to the well and learned exactly where his quarry lay, and yet was turned back at the door by the Spirit of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD hides His own not always by concealment, but often in plain sight, under the shadow of His hand. The enemy may learn the very place and still be undone. It is not our hiddenness that keeps us, but our God, who ordereth even the pursuer’s steps.
roots_summary: The name is of uncertain root, perhaps from a word meaning to look out or watch; it marks a well on the way to Ramah.
roots_lines: Sechu renders Hebrew Seku, a place near Ramah.
Some derive it from a root meaning to look out or observe, hence a lookout.
The Scripture notes it chiefly for its great well.
It lay on Saul’s road as he pursued David toward Ramah.
The name endures only in the story of a pursuer turned back.
usage: Saul came to the great well that is in Sechu and asked for David.
At Sechu the enemy learned the place, and still could not prevail.
The well of Sechu teaches that God keeps His own in plain sight.

etymology: Hebrew Shen, “a tooth,” hence a jutting crag or pointed rock; the landmark between which and Mizpeh Samuel set up the stone Ebenezer.
biblical_def: After the LORD had thundered upon the Philistines and Israel had driven them from Mizpeh, Samuel took a stone and set it between Mizpeh and Shen, and called the name of it Ebenezer, saying, “Hitherto hath the LORD helped us” (1Sa 7:12). Shen, “the tooth,” likely a jutting crag, is named only to fix the spot where the stone of help was raised; yet in that humble office it shares the memorial for ever. Samuel did what the saints have always done: he marked the mercy with a monument, that the deliverance might not be forgotten. “Hitherto” looks two ways — backward over all the road the LORD has led, and forward in hope, for the God who has helped thus far will not forsake His people now. The stone could not save; it could only remember; but a remembering people is a thankful people, and a thankful people is a believing people. We are prone to forget His benefits, to let past mercies slip as the deliverance grows old; therefore the LORD would have us set up our Ebenezers, keeping the account of His helps between our Mizpehs and our Shens. Every answered prayer, every rescue, every hitherto, is a stone to be set up and named; and the sum of them all is the faithfulness of a God who changeth not, whose help of yesterday is the surety of His help unto the end.
webster_summary: The crag between which and Mizpeh Samuel set up the stone Ebenezer, saying, Hitherto hath the LORD helped us (1Sa 7:12); a landmark of the memorial that keeps the account of God’s mercies.
webster_full: SHEN, a rock or crag near Mizpeh, the name signifying “a tooth.”
Between Mizpeh and Shen Samuel set the stone of help (1Sa 7:12).
He called it Ebenezer, saying, Hitherto hath the LORD helped us.
The name fixes the spot of a great deliverance from the Philistines.
It teaches the saints to mark the mercies of God with a memorial.
scriptures: Then Samuel took a stone, and set it between Mizpeh and Shen, and called the name of it Ebenezer, saying, Hitherto hath the LORD helped us.
And Laban said, This heap is a witness between me and thee this day. Therefore was the name of it called Galeed;

corruption_summary: The crag by which Samuel raised his Ebenezer; it recovers the duty to remember and mark the mercies of God along the way.
corruption_paragraphs: Shen is a jutting rock near Mizpeh, named in Scripture for one office only: to fix the place where Samuel set the stone Ebenezer after the rout of the Philistines. In that humble service it shares the memorial for ever.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the marking of mercy. We are prone to forget the benefits of the LORD as the deliverance grows old; therefore Samuel set up his stone, that a remembering people might be a thankful and believing people. Set up your Ebenezers between your Mizpehs and your Shens, for the God who helped hitherto will help to the end.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew shen, a tooth, applied to a sharp or jutting rock.
roots_lines: Shen renders Hebrew shen, “a tooth.”
The word is used of the teeth of man and beast, and of ivory.
By figure it names a sharp crag or tooth-like rock, as here.
It marks the western bound of Samuel’s Ebenezer stone.
The place is remembered wholly for the memorial raised beside it.
usage: Samuel set the stone between Mizpeh and Shen and called it Ebenezer.
Shen is named only to fix the place of the stone of help.
Between our Mizpehs and Shens we too should raise an Ebenezer.

etymology: Hebrew Se'irah, “the wooded” or “shaggy place,” from sa'ir, hairy or rough, akin to Seir; the district in the hill country of Ephraim to which Ehud escaped.
biblical_def: When Ehud had slain Eglon the king of Moab, that had oppressed Israel eighteen years, he made his escape while the servants tarried; “and passed beyond the quarries, and escaped unto Seirath” (Jdg 3:26). Seirath, in the hill country of Ephraim, was the place of rallying; for no sooner was the deliverer come than “he blew a trumpet in the mountain of Ephraim, and the children of Israel went down with him from the mount, and he before them” (Jdg 3:27). The trumpet of Seirath is the trumpet of deliverance that follows the fall of the tyrant. First the oppressor is smitten in secret, then the summons soundeth abroad, and the people who had groaned under Moab now go down to the battle with their captain before them. So the LORD worketh salvation for His church: He raiseth up a deliverer of His own choosing, cutteth down the mighty in the day of His appointing, and then gathereth His people by the sound of the trumpet to enter into the victory He hath wrought. Ehud, left-handed and unlikely, is a figure of the weak things God chooseth to confound the mighty; and the trumpet he blew foreshadoweth the gospel summons that goeth forth after a greater Deliverer hath overthrown a greater tyrant. When the strong man is bound, the trumpet soundeth; and the redeemed go down after their Leader, who is before them, into the liberty He hath purchased.
webster_summary: The district in mount Ephraim whither Ehud escaped after slaying Eglon, and whence he blew the trumpet to rally Israel (Jdg 3:26–27); a witness to the LORD raising a deliverer and the trumpet of deliverance after the tyrant falls.
webster_full: SEIRATH, a wooded district in mount Ephraim, whither Ehud fled.
He escaped thither past the quarries after slaying Eglon of Moab (Jdg 3:26).
From that place he blew a trumpet to gather Israel (Jdg 3:27).
It marks the rallying-point after the oppressor was smitten in secret.
It foreshadows the summons that follows the overthrow of a greater tyrant.

Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD; and the people whom he hath chosen for his own inheritance.
Psa 46:6

corruption_summary: The place of Ehud’s escape and rallying trumpet; it recovers the truth that God raises deliverers and sounds the trumpet of freedom after the tyrant falls.
corruption_paragraphs: Seirath is a wooded district in the hill country of Ephraim, remembered as the place whither Ehud escaped after slaying Eglon, and whence he blew the trumpet that gathered Israel to the battle. It is a name of deliverance.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD raiseth up deliverers of His own choosing, cutteth down the mighty in His appointed day, and then gathereth His people by the trumpet to enter the victory He hath wrought. Ehud, left-handed and unlikely, is a figure of the weak things God chooseth to confound the mighty.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew sa'ir, hairy or shaggy, hence a wooded or rough district; akin to the name Seir.
roots_lines: Seirath renders Hebrew Se'irah, “the wooded place.”
The root sa'ir means hairy, rough, or shaggy.
By figure it names a place thick with wood or brush.
The same root gives the name Seir, the rough hill country of Edom.
It lay within the mountain of Ephraim, whence Ehud sounded the trumpet.
usage: Ehud escaped unto Seirath after the tyrant fell.
From Seirath the trumpet sounded, and Israel went down to war.
The trumpet of Seirath is the summons that follows deliverance.
